nameStory: The house centipede gets its straightforward name from its favorite hangout spot – your home! Unlike most centipedes that prefer outdoor hideaways, this Mediterranean native has become the ultimate indoor roommate, scurrying through basements, bathrooms, and closets across New England.
description: The house centipede is a fast-moving arthropod with a yellowish-gray body and an impressive collection of up to 15 pairs of extremely long, delicate legs. Despite its name suggesting 100 legs, this centipede actually has far fewer – but what it lacks in quantity, it makes up for in speed and agility. These beneficial predators hunt down household pests like flies, moths, and spiders, making them helpful (if startling) housemates. They typically measure about 1-2 inches long, though their long legs make them appear much larger.

idTips.label: Extremely long legs
idTips.description: The legs are extraordinarily long and thin, almost thread-like, extending far beyond the body length and giving the creature a delicate, almost ethereal appearance as it moves

idTips.label: Yellowish-gray coloration
idTips.description: The body displays muted yellowish-gray tones with darker stripes running lengthwise, creating a somewhat translucent appearance

idTips.label: Lightning-fast movement
idTips.description: Moves with startling speed in a fluid, wave-like motion that seems to flow across surfaces rather than run – often freezing completely when spotted by light

idTips.label: Flattened body shape
idTips.description: The body appears somewhat flattened and segmented, allowing it to squeeze into surprisingly narrow cracks and crevices

idTips.label: Long antennae
idTips.description: Two prominent antennae extend forward from the head, almost as long as the body itself, constantly moving and sensing the environment

idTips.label: Legs that break easily
idTips.description: The delicate legs break off readily when grabbed – you might find detached legs still twitching, which helps the centipede escape predators

habitat: House centipedes are most commonly found inside human dwellings throughout New England, particularly in damp areas like basements, bathrooms, crawl spaces, and laundry rooms. They prefer areas with high humidity and often hide under sinks, in shower stalls, or behind washing machines during the day. While originally outdoor creatures, they've adapted so well to indoor life that they're now more commonly spotted inside than in their natural outdoor habitats of leaf litter and rock crevices.

seasonality.spring: House centipedes become more active as temperatures warm, often appearing more frequently as they hunt for emerging insects and begin their breeding season indoors.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most likely to be spotted darting across bathroom floors or basement walls, actively hunting the abundant insects that also seek indoor shelter during hot weather.
seasonality.fall: Remain active indoors as outdoor temperatures drop, often becoming more noticeable as they move to warmer areas of the house and continue hunting for overwintering insects.
seasonality.winter: Still active in heated homes, though slower-moving in cooler areas – this is when they're most likely to be found in warm spots near furnaces, water heaters, or heated bathrooms.

funFact: House centipedes can live for up to 7 years and don't actually start life with all their legs – they're born with just 4 pairs and grow additional pairs each time they molt, kind of like collecting a new set of running shoes with every growth spurt!
confusionNotes: House centipedes are most commonly confused with silverfish, but remember: centipedes are the "runners" with all those long legs streaming behind them, while silverfish are the "wigglers" with just 6 legs and a fish-like wiggling motion. If it looks like it's wearing a grass skirt made of legs, it's a centipede!
contextualKnowledge: Despite their fearsome appearance and the fact that they are venomous predators, house centipedes are completely harmless to humans – their tiny fangs can't penetrate human skin, and they're actually beneficial because they hunt down truly problematic household pests like cockroaches, bed bugs, and termites.
compareHints: The house centipede is the only member of its genus found in New England, making it unique among local centipedes. Unlike the shorter-legged soil centipedes found under logs and stones outdoors, house centipedes have distinctively long, delicate legs and prefer indoor environments. Their speed and leg length make them unmistakable compared to any other centipede species in the region.
